title: rootless: container silently runs without a cgroup when cgroup creation fails, then podman stop can't stop it with --pid=host
body:
### Issue Description

   I ran into this through Distrobox: `distrobox ephemeral` leaves the container behind, because stopping it fails with `given PID did not die within timeout`
 (https://github.com/89luca89/distrobox/issues/1939). Distrobox runs its containers with `--pid=host`.

   What happens, as far as I can tell:

   1. Rootless with cgroupfs and no `--cgroup-parent`, Podman leaves `linux.cgroupsPath` empty in the OCI spec and lets the runtime pick a cgroup.
   2. If crun can't create that cgroup, it ignores the error and starts the container without one
 ([cgroup.c#L339-L365](https://github.com/containers/crun/blob/8af97a355f027c6e2ed9f4f8a88fd563fcc7beda/src/libcrun/cgroup.c#L339-L365)).
   3. With `--pid=host`, `podman stop` asks the runtime to kill all processes. crun does that through the cgroup, and with no cgroup it returns success without killing anything
 ([cgroup-utils.c#L1031-L1040](https://github.com/containers/crun/blob/8af97a355f027c6e2ed9f4f8a88fd563fcc7beda/src/libcrun/cgroup-utils.c#L1031-L1040)).
   4. Podman waits and times out.

   So the container ends up with neither a cgroup nor its own PID namespace, which is exactly the combination Podman refuses when you ask for it explicitly (`--cgroups=disabled
 --pid=host` is rejected).

### Steps to reproduce the issue

   The cgroup creation failure can be simulated by making `/sys/fs/cgroup` read-only in a private mount namespace:

   ```
   podman unshare unshare --mount sh -c '
     mount --bind /sys/fs/cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup
     mount -o remount,bind,ro /sys/fs/cgroup
     podman --cgroup-manager=cgroupfs run -d --name test --pid=host --pids-limit=-1 \
         alpine sh -c "sleep 600 & exec sleep 600"
     podman --cgroup-manager=cgroupfs stop -t 1 test
   '
   ```

### Describe the results you received

   The container starts. `stop` fails after the timeout:

   ```
   level=warning msg="StopSignal SIGTERM failed to stop container test in 1 seconds, resorting to SIGKILL"
   Error: given PID did not die within timeout
   ```

   Both sleep processes are still running. `podman rm --force` fails the same way. `podman kill` kills the main process, but the background `sleep` survives and gets reparented to
 conmon.

   With `--pid=private` instead of `--pid=host` the container stops fine.

### Describe the results you expected

Since cgroups are enabled, I'd expect `podman run` to fail when the cgroup can't be created, instead of starting a container that can't be stopped later.

### Podman in a container

No

### Privileged Or Rootless

Rootless

### Upstream Latest Release

Yes

### Additional environment details

Podman 6.1.4, conmon 2.2.1, crun 1.29.1, cgroup v2. The reporter of the Distrobox issue is on Void musl; I reproduced it on Gentoo.

### Additional information

   I looked at whether conmon could just track and kill the processes itself when there's no cgroup. Linux has `PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER`, so orphaned processes end up under conmon,
 but I couldn't find anything like FreeBSD's `procctl(PROC_REAP_KILL)` that signals all descendants of a reaper in one go. Without a cgroup or a PID namespace you'd have to walk the
 process tree and signal each process, which races with fork. So I think the existing rule (cgroup or private PID namespace) is right, and the bug is that the runtime fallback
 bypasses it.

   runc also starts the container without a cgroup in this setup, so this isn't specific to crun.

   VM runtimes like krun are a bit different: the workload runs inside the guest, so the PID namespace check doesn't protect anything there. I think `--cgroups=disabled --pid=host`
 could be allowed for runtimes that are in both `runtime_supports_kvm` and `runtime_supports_nocgroup`. With cgroups enabled they should still fail the same way as crun/runc.

   I have a fix for this: Podman creates the cgroup itself before calling the runtime (trying the root first, then next to its own cgroup) and passes the path explicitly, so the
 runtime has no fallback to take. PRs coming.

comments.body: we must fix it in crun, we can't ignore cgroups failures if `--pid=host`
and if you are going to open a PR in crun, please make sure to use your real name and email address for the author and DCO line.

> 6\. and if you are going to open a PR in crun, please make sure to use your real name and email address for the author and DCO line.

Ok, thanks for reminder, I will
Just note for myself here: runc, youki, ocijail need check also

> 5\. we must fix it in crun, we can't ignore cgroups failures if `--pid=host`

BTW because I previously noticed that conmon also attempts to run within a cgroup, so I believe it is more appropriate for Podman to handle this.

Moreover, I assumed that `crun` intentionally allows this behavior, so I also implemented a fallback mechanism to kill the process tree, however, it is not possible to implement this mechanism reliably, as this functionality does not exist in the Linux kernel.

@giuseppe I have one more question: do you think we could add support for launching backends that rely on a VM runtime using both `--pid=host` and `--cgroups=disabled`? That will allow normal user who not requiring any special permissions use podman and it doesn't seem to have any downsides.

ocijail (FreeBSD), following up on my note above. Tested on FreeBSD 15.0 with podman 5.8.6 and ocijail 0.6.1. `podman stop`, `stop` with an init that ignores TERM, `rm -f` and `--pid=host` all return, and no process of the container is left, because `ocijail delete` removes the jail with `jail_remove(2)`. Podman does call `ocijail kill --all`, but ocijail ignores `--all` for now, so the other processes get SIGKILL at delete instead of the stop signal. Related open PRs (each one's new test fails on main and passes with the PR):

- https://github.com/dfr/ocijail/pull/26 Implement kill --all
- https://github.com/dfr/ocijail/pull/32 Detect stopped containers whose pid has been reused
- https://github.com/dfr/ocijail/pull/37 Don't act on a jail or pid which no longer belongs to the container
